figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Effective use of context is essential for accurate time series forecasting. In crude oil price forecasting, textual context (e.g., recession fears on March 9) aligns with sudden price shifts. Our approach, Context as Covariates (CoCo), leverages this context to produce accurate forecasts, while unimodal models such as Chronos2 fail to capture context-induced trends.
figures.headline: CoCo produces accurate crude oil forecasts from recession-fear news, while Chronos2 misses context-induced trends.
citing_sentences: These contextual forecasting examples across domains show that the textual context is deeply intertwined with real-world time series and can provide signals about future changes that are not captured by past numerical values alone (check Figure 1).

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: CoCo outperforms SOTA TSFMs (Chronos2) and closed-source LLMs (GPT-4o) across datasets from diverse domains. CoCo effectively utilizes LLMs to distill textual annotations into usable forecast covariates that guide powerful TSFMs to generate accurate forecasts.
figures.headline: CoCo outperforms Chronos2 and GPT-4o across domains, reaching up to 70% improvement over GPT-4o in traffic forecasting.
citing_sentences: CoCo outperforms SOTA TSFMs and LLMs across 30 datasets and 95 settings (Figure 5) spanning finance, weather, macroeconomics, traffic, and security domains, achieving up to 70% improvement over GPT-4o in traffic forecasting (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Training on synthetic annotations yields real-world multimodal gains. Using pharmaceutical sales data annotated with both real news and synthetic text, a SARIMA model with sentiment features achieves similar MAE when trained on synthetic versus real annotations, as both encode the same domain-agnostic forecast trends, thereby enabling sim-to-real transfer.
figures.headline: A SARIMA model with sentiment features reaches similar MAE whether trained on synthetic or real annotations.
citing_sentences: We validate this observation using a toy example (Figure 3).
The results in Figure 3 show that the TRTR and TSTR MAEs are very similar, thereby establishing the veracity of our sim-to-real approach for multimodal forecasting, for this specific toy scenario.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Context as Covariates (CoCo) Description. The LLM $\theta_{\mathrm{LLM}}$ takes the numerical history $X^{H}_{t}$ (blue) and textual context $S_{t}$ (violet) as input and produces a forecast covariate $M_{t}$ (Equation 5, brown) and a rollout-based confidence covariate $C_{t}$ (Equation 6, maroon), which are concatenated with $X^{H}_{t}$ and passed to Chronos2 for multivariate forecasting. Our key technical intuition is to utilize the confidence covariate (obtained from the per-step variance in the LLM’s predictions) to teach Chronos2 when to trust the LLM and when not to trust it (low variance $\rightarrow$ trust the LLM, as text induces a more decisive forecast).
figures.headline: The LLM's forecast and rollout-based confidence covariates are concatenated with history and passed to Chronos2.
citing_sentences: We introduce CoCo (Context as Covariates), a multimodal forecasting framework that combines LLMs’ ability to interpret text with TSFMs’ numerical precision (Figure 4).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: CoCo improves over unimodal and multimodal fine-tuning approaches, including SOTA TSFMs on real-world multimodal datasets. CoCo (ours) achieves the best average rank and mean MAE across 30 datasets (95 settings) spanning diverse domains and context lengths against 26 (TimeOmni omitted for scale) approaches. These gains demonstrate the effectiveness of GRPO-based fine-tuning along with our novel two-step fine-tuning.
figures.headline: CoCo has the best average rank and mean MAE against 26 approaches across 30 datasets and 95 settings.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 shows that incorporating text embeddings into SOTA multivariate forecasting models does not necessarily yield multimodal gains, even when the text clearly contains useful information.

CoCo outperforms SOTA TSFMs and LLMs across 30 datasets and 95 settings (Figure 5) spanning finance, weather, macroeconomics, traffic, and security domains, achieving up to 70% improvement over GPT-4o in traffic forecasting (Figure 2).
We refer the readers to Tables 1 and 2, and Figure 5.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: CoCo generalizes across model choices. MAE improvement over each numerical-only M-TSFM baseline on Media Cloud (64-16 setting).
figures.headline: CoCo improves MAE over each numerical-only M-TSFM baseline on the Media Cloud 64-16 setting.
citing_sentences: Tables 25 and 26, and Figure 6 demonstrate that CoCo is not specific to Qwen3-4B or Chronos2.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: (Left) CoCo consistently outperforms SOTA unimodal models (Chronos2) when text is useful (Q5–Q9) and underperforms when it is not (Q1–Q3). Text usefulness is defined as the relative MAE improvement of the LLM forecast when the context $S_{t}$ is provided versus withheld. (Right) Furthermore, for the set of windows where text is useful, CoCo significantly outperforms unimodal models when the rollout variance from the LLM (Confidence $C_{t}$) is very low.
figures.headline: CoCo beats Chronos2 when text is useful and trails it when text is not, and significantly outperforms it at very low rollout confidence.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 (left) shows that text usefulness is a strong indicator of CoCo’s gains.
Figure 7 (right) shows that when text is highly useful, performance peaks at high LLM confidence and degrades as confidence decreases.
When the text is misleading, the LLM can generate confidently incorrect covariates that Chronos2 cannot fully correct, thereby degrading performance (Table 21, Figure 7 (left)).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Real and synthetic annotations contain similar predictive powers to estimate the future. The significant overlap of cosine similarity distributions between the true and the predicted forecast descriptions for synthetic and real annotations validates our synthetic annotation strategy. For the real cosine similarity distribution, we compare the normalized BERT embeddings for the domain-agnostic forecast predictions from real text with the true domain-agnostic forecast description. Similarly, for the synthetic cosine similarity distribution, we compare the normalized BERT embeddings for the domain-agnostic forecast predictions from synthetic text with the true domain-agnostic forecast description. For this experiment, we consider the Media Cloud datasets for which the real annotations are available, and we generated synthetic annotations for those datasets.
figures.headline: Cosine similarity distributions for real and synthetic annotations overlap significantly on the Media Cloud datasets.
citing_sentences: The significant overlap in resulting distributions (Figure 8) indicates synthetic annotations capture the forecast with levels of uncertainty similar to those observed in real context.
To justify small $\varepsilon_{s}$, we refer to Figure 8.
In Figure 8, we show the strong overlap in cosine similarity distributions between the embeddings of the verbal description of the forecast predictions derived from real and synthetic annotations.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Real and synthetic annotations contain similar domain-agnostic descriptions, but differ in semantics. Here, we show the t-SNE plots for concatenated embeddings of real and synthetic annotations. We consider the Media Cloud datasets for which the real annotations are available, and we generated synthetic annotations for those datasets. On the left, we compare the embeddings of real domain-agnostic predictions concatenated with true forecast descriptions against the synthetic counterpart. Similarly, on the right, we compare the embeddings of the real domain-specific prediction concatenated with the true forecast descriptions against the synthetic counterpart. Note that there is near-perfect overlap in the domain-agnostic case and clear separation in the domain-specific case. This conveys that for the same true forecast description (through concatenation), the domain-agnostic predictions overlap indicating that real and synthetic annotations provide similar domain-agnostic prediction. In contrast, the domain-specific predictions vary significantly, indicating that both real and synthetic domain-specific predictions have different semantic constructions.
figures.headline: Real and synthetic annotations overlap almost perfectly in domain-agnostic embeddings but separate in domain-specific ones.
citing_sentences: Additionally, our claim of real and synthetic annotations capturing similar domain-agnostic predictions in Section 4 is visually depicted in Figure 9.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Average GRPO training reward $r_{t}$ (Eq. 7) over training steps, computed as the mean over $N_{\text{rollouts}}$ rollouts per prompt in a batch. The reward increases steadily reflecting that the LLM progressively learns to generate forecast covariates $M_{t}$ that provide better forecasts ($\theta_{\mathrm{M-TSFM}}(X^{H}_{t}||M_{t})$) relative to the unimodal baseline ($\theta_{\mathrm{M-TSFM}}(X^{H}_{t})$).
figures.headline: The average GRPO training reward rises steadily as the LLM learns covariates that beat the unimodal baseline.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Qwen3 provides realistic textual annotations. Here, we show samples of annotations generated by Qwen3-30b-A3B-Instruct-2507 [9] for gasoline prices in the United States for the year 2022. Note that the text generated is relevant to the domain queried and foreshadows the trend in the numerical data. In the plot, the green portion indicates an increasing trend and the red portion indicates a decreasing trend.
figures.headline: Qwen3-30B annotations for 2022 gasoline prices in the United States are relevant and foreshadow the numerical trend.
citing_sentences: We propose a scalable approach to address the scarcity of multi-domain multimodal datasets by generating textual annotations for real-world time series using LLMs, motivated by the following key intuition: given numerical trajectories and domain descriptions, LLMs can produce semantically meaningful explanations for observed temporal trends (see Figure 11).

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Our approach to generate textual annotations, for real-world time series datasets, extracted from the news articles that are scraped from the internet. Let us consider the task of generating textual annotations for the NVIDIA stock price dataset. First, we use the Media Cloud API to extract the relevant news articles between two successive timestamps $t-1$ and $t$. These news articles are summarized into Key Events and Facts and Predictive Information by an LLM. This summary is treated as the text annotation for the timestamp $t$.
figures.headline: Media Cloud articles between consecutive timestamps are summarized by an LLM into each timestamp's annotation.
citing_sentences: Media Cloud For the curation of the text for the new evaluation datasets, we leveraged the Media Cloud API for news articles with timestamps and used the pipeline shown in Figure 12 to obtain text annotations on a daily basis.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Comparison of standalone forecasting performance of LLMs. The plot shows the %-improvement in the MAE over the base Qwen3-4B model across the same 38 settings as Table 22. We observe that the CoCo fine-tuned Qwen3-4B outperforms larger and closed-source LLMs as a standalone forecaster.
figures.headline: CoCo fine-tuned Qwen3-4B beats larger and closed-source LLMs as a standalone forecaster across 38 settings.
citing_sentences: The fine-tuned Qwen3-4B also outperforms the larger zero-shot LLMs as a standalone forecaster (Figure 13).

abstract: Textual information is ubiquitous in real-world time series datasets, appearing as news, reports, and annotations that hold key predictive signals not deducible from numerical history alone. Large Language Models (LLMs) interpret text but lack numerical precision, while Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) are quantitatively accurate but cannot reason about the effects of text. Moreover, the lack of large-scale paired multimodal datasets limits progress in bridging this gap. In this work, we address this challenge by providing a scalable approach for generating realistic multimodal datasets by annotating real-world time series with LLMs. Building on this, we propose Context as Covariates (CoCo), a forecasting framework in which an LLM distills its textual reasoning into numerically grounded forecast and confidence covariates that guide a TSFM backbone, thereby exploiting the strengths of both LLMs and TSFMs. We align the two models in stages, first fine-tuning the LLM via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a reward tied to covariate-induced improvement in forecasting performance, and then fine-tuning the TSFM on covariates generated by the aligned LLM. Our experiments show that models trained on our synthetic multimodal corpus generalize to real benchmarks spanning finance, economics, weather, traffic, and security. Notably, CoCo with Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 as the LLM and Chronos2 as the TSFM achieves up to 12% MAE improvement over state-of-the-art TSFMs and LLM forecasters, such as GPT-4o. Code, checkpoints, and the evaluation datasets are publicly available.

sections.body: The section argues that text such as news and analyst notes holds predictive signal that numerical history lacks. It states that TimesFM and Chronos2 use only numerical inputs, and that adding text embeddings to them does not necessarily help. It names two barriers: few aligned multimodal samples in existing datasets, and LLM-centric methods that neglect TSFM forecasting strengths. The contributions are a synthetic annotation pipeline, the CoCo architecture with staged fine-tuning, and gains across 30 datasets and 95 settings, with up to 70% improvement over GPT-4o in traffic forecasting.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Textual context carries forecasting signals that numerical foundation models cannot use, motivating a paired LLM and TSFM design.

sections.body: This section reviews text-aided forecasting in two groups: zero-shot methods that prompt LLMs with serialized series, and training-based methods that fine-tune LLMs, align embeddings, or fuse modalities. It argues that finance has abundant time-varying text, while healthcare and other settings typically provide static descriptors. It states that TimeMMD and Context-Is-Key are used for benchmarking because of their small sizes. The authors summarize that prior work focuses on LLMs as forecasters, relies on dataset-specific training, and does not exploit SOTA TSFMs. Their setup is zero-shot and domain-agnostic, combining LLMs and TSFMs. Appendix A gives a detailed discussion.
sections.heading: Related Works
sections.headline: Prior text-aided forecasters are domain-specific, LLM-centric, or ignore TSFMs, so this work targets a zero-shot, domain-agnostic setup.

sections.body: Section 3 defines the unimodal case as a model that maps a historical numerical window of length $l$ to a forecast of horizon $h$. The multimodal case adds a textual annotation for each timestamp in the context, capped at a maximum number of tokens per annotation. Each annotation may summarize past values and give cues for the future. The multimodal model takes the history and the annotations as input and produces the forecast. The section sets up notation only and reports no experiments.
sections.heading: Problem Formulation
sections.headline: Multimodal forecasting is defined as mapping numerical history and per-timestamp text annotations to a future forecast.

sections.body: The section generates annotations by sampling random fixed-length windows and giving Qwen3-30B the values, timestamps and dataset description. The prompt asks for per-timestamp events that explain the history, plus speculative future descriptions without numeric forecasts. Realism is checked by comparing BERT embedding cosine similarity of predicted and true future descriptions for real and synthetic text (Figure 8). A SARIMA toy example with sentiment features gives similar MAE on real and synthetic annotations. The authors note that synthetic annotations use future values during generation, unlike causal real annotations, and that the bounded transfer gap depends on encoder alignment.
sections.heading: Synthetic Multimodal Dataset Generation
sections.headline: An LLM generates annotations from numerical windows that resemble real text in forecast-trend similarity, supporting sim-to-real transfer.

sections.body: CoCo has the LLM produce a text-aware median forecast, $m$, and a confidence covariate from the spread of N rollouts. The forecast covariate places a noisy copy of the history before the LLM forecast so the TSFM can read it as a next-step predictor. The confidence covariate is the rollout variance divided by the history variance, so low values mean high confidence. The LLM is first fine-tuned with GRPO against a frozen M-TSFM, with a reward in (0,1) that approaches 1 when the covariate improves forecasts and is 0.5 when it does not. The M-TSFM is then fine-tuned with MSE on covariates from the tuned LLM. The confidence covariate is excluded from the reward because of rollout cost.
sections.heading: Context as Covariates
sections.headline: CoCo feeds LLM forecast and confidence covariates to a TSFM, with the LLM tuned by GRPO and the TSFM tuned afterward.

sections.body: Training uses 36,826 synthetic time series datasets (~12.4M rows) and about 150,000 rows of real finance annotations. Evaluation covers 30 datasets with over 16,719 samples, at context lengths 64, 128 and 256 and forecast length 16. In Table 1, CoCo has a mean MAE of 0.719, against 0.735 for TiRex, 0.745 for Chronos2, 0.749 for TimesFM2.5 and 0.836 for GPT-4o. The text says CoCo outperforms TiRex in 60/95 settings. The stated limitations are inference cost, since CoCo needs extra LLM inference that Table 29 compares with unimodal TSFMs, and degraded results when the text is misleading, because the LLM can produce confidently incorrect covariates.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: CoCo with Qwen3-4B and Chronos2 has the best mean MAE, 0.719, across 30 datasets and 95 settings.

sections.body: The conclusion summarizes two contributions: a recipe for generating large-scale multimodal time series datasets with text as the alternative modality, and the CoCo architecture for adding textual information to SOTA TSFM forecasts. It reports up to 12% MAE improvement over SOTA TSFMs and LLM forecasters. The authors name two limits. The model can be misled by unreliable text, so they propose a reliability check based on the relationship between text and history. The current training is sequential, so they propose exploring joint fine-tuning of the LLM and the M-TSFM.
sections.heading: Conclusion and Future Work
sections.headline: Future work proposes a text reliability check and joint fine-tuning, because CoCo degrades when text is misleading.

sections.body: The appendix extends the related work and gives proofs for Lemma 4.3 and Theorem 4.4. It reports a probe comparison of real and synthetic annotations, noting that prefix-only annotations give lower direction accuracy and that linear probes are a limitation. Table 28 shows that fine-tuning both components gives mean MAE 0.719, against 0.732 with the LLM alone and 0.724 with the M-TSFM alone. Table 29 gives inference latency, with CoCo at 280.07 ms per sample. Appendix I lists the prompts, and Appendix J covers societal impact and the sensitivity to misleading text.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, theorem proofs, probe and ablation tables, latency, prompts and societal impact.
